Empirically, this is not a graceful degradation; Wei et al.'s work on safety fine-tuning (and subsequent jailbreak literature) shows that safety behaviors in instruction-tuned models are surprisingly brittle and concentrated in specific layers — typically later MLP layers — meaning that a coding adapter which modifies those same layers can actively suppress safety-relevant activations rather than merely failing to reinforce them, producing outputs worse than the base model on safety metrics. The equilibrium collapses to the defender needing to check all layers simultaneously with no leakage of pass/fail information — which means the safety check result cannot be returned to the submitter at all, converting adapter onboarding into a black-box certification process where the adversary receives only a binary "accepted/rejected" signal with no timing information, analogous to how cryptographic oracles must be rate-limited and output-sanitized to prevent oracle attacks. Even that is insufficient if the adversary can submit adapters and then query the deployed system with crafted prompts, because inference-time outputs constitute a high-bandwidth side channel that reveals far more about which layers are active than any onboarding check — the true equilibrium requires that adversarial adapter submission and inference-time probing be treated as a joint attack surface, which no current multi-tenant serving system architecture addresses.
